tldr: By combining a lightweight semantic bird's-eye-view (BEV) representation with trajectory alignment, zero-shot off-road autonomous driving was achieved on two real vehicles at speeds up to 33.6 km/h, without relying on high-fidelity physics or graphics simulators.
hero_caption: The overall pipeline of MILER. During simulation, reinforcement learning is trained on a semantic bird's-eye view (BEV) generated from Perlin noise and a simplified bicycle model. During real-world driving, the BEV of the real environment generated by BEVFusion is fed in while the real vehicle tracks the trajectory of the virtual vehicle, simultaneously bridging the Sim-to-Real gap in both perception and control.
overview:
Reinforcement learning (RL) holds great promise for autonomous driving. However, in unstructured environments without paved roads or lane markings (such as off-road terrain), real-world trial-and-error learning is not feasible due to safety concerns. At the same time, directly transferring policies learned in simulation to real vehicles—known as "Sim-to-Real transfer"—has been extremely challenging due to diverse visual appearances and complex vehicle dynamics. Conventional approaches have attempted to bridge this gap by building photorealistic 3D simulators and high-fidelity vehicle physics models, but doing so incurs enormous costs.

To solve this, the authors completely discard heavy 3D graphics rendering and complex physics computations, instead creating a custom lightweight simulator that operates purely on a semantic bird's-eye-view (BEV) and a simple 2-wheel kinematic model (bicycle model). Perception is abstracted into just four classes: "Drivable", "Semi-drivable", "Non-drivable", and "None" (unknown). Furthermore, during deployment, the BEV estimated by the real vehicle is geometrically transformed into the virtual vehicle's coordinate frame, and the real vehicle tracks the virtual vehicle's trajectory via "trajectory alignment." This eliminates the Sim-to-Real gap across both perception and control.

In experiments, the system was evaluated on a 3.0 km test track featuring obstacles, sharp hairpin curves, and tall grass, using two test vehicles with different physical specifications. Without any human intervention, the vehicles covered a total of 17.3 km, achieving smooth autonomous driving exceeding 30 km/h (up to 33.6 km/h)—a first for vehicle-scale reinforcement learning in unstructured environments. The system also demonstrated remarkable efficiency, with an inference time of just 1.9 ms on an edge computer (Jetson AGX Orin).
contributions: Developed a fast semantic mid-level representation (MLR) simulator that eliminates 3D rendering and complex physics modeling, relying instead on Perlin noise-based semantic grid maps and a bicycle model.
Proposed MILER, a framework that zero-shot transfers policies trained in abstract simulation to real vehicles by combining perception geometric alignment with trajectory alignment for control.

Achieved a top speed of 33.6 km/h without interventions across 17.3 km of off-road driving experiments with two real vehicles, breaking the 30 km/h barrier for the first time in real-vehicle reinforcement learning in unstructured environments.

sections.heading: Why lightweight mid-level representations and RL work for unstructured autonomous driving
sections.summary: Because trial-and-error on real hardware is dangerous in unstructured off-road environments, simulation training is essential, yet the Sim-to-Real gap has been a major barrier. This work introduces MILER, which combines a semantic mid-level representation (MLR) simulator with a trajectory-alignment strategy to deploy on real vehicles without additional fine-tuning.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is an appealing approach capable of self-learning control policies with superhuman potential. However, carrying out transfer learning or repeated trial-and-error on real hardware in unstructured environments like off-road terrains is unacceptable due to safety risks such as collisions. As a result, training in simulated environments is standard, but faithfully replicating complex real-world physics and diverse visual appearances inside a simulator is exceptionally difficult.

MILER smartly bypasses this Sim-to-Real challenge. On the perception side, instead of directly simulating raw camera or LiDAR data, inputs are aggregated into a semantic bird's-eye view (BEV) as a "mid-level representation." The simulator uses procedurally generated maps inspired by Minecraft terrain generation and models vehicle motion using only a simple 2-wheel kinematic model (bicycle model).

During real-vehicle deployment, the real-world BEV generated from onboard sensors via BEVFusion is aligned to the virtual vehicle's coordinate system. The virtual vehicle moves according to the actions computed by the RL policy, and the real vehicle tracks it using a "trajectory-alignment" approach. This minimizes domain gaps in vehicle dynamics and perception, enabling zero-shot deployment across two different real vehicles without any post-tuning.

sections.heading: How this differs from prior work: breaking free from heavy simulators
sections.summary: Conventional Sim-to-Real research has predominantly focused on building photorealistic graphics and high-fidelity vehicle physics models. This work sets itself apart by applying mid-level representations—originally popularized in urban driving—to off-road settings, bridging both perception and control through geometry and control engineering.
sections.details:
Sim-to-Real research in off-road and unstructured environments remains far more limited compared to urban autonomous driving. While imitation learning and direct RL on real vehicles have been explored, training and evaluating without simulators is unrealistic in systems where safety is the top priority.

Challenges in Sim-to-Real transfer broadly split into two areas: perception and actuation (vehicle control and dynamics).

- **Actuation transfer**: At higher speeds, vehicle vibrations, latencies, and friction make behavior unstable. Prior work relied on creating detailed physical models or learning vehicle models from real driving data. In contrast, this work adopts "trajectory alignment," having the real vehicle track a simulated virtual vehicle, making detailed physical modeling entirely unnecessary.
- **Perception transfer**: Past efforts relied on high-fidelity simulators (such as CARLA) to make camera and LiDAR rendering look realistic. However, modeling textures and lighting demands immense effort. While some studies use intermediate representations (like BEV or segmentation images), they still relied on detailed high-fidelity simulators.

While abstract representation simulators such as Nocturne and CommonRoad exist for urban environments, this work is the first to fully apply a semantic mid-level representation simulator to reinforcement learning in unstructured environments.

sections.heading: Inside MILER: simulator, state representation, training, and real-world deployment
sections.summary: A bicycle model is driven across BEV maps procedurally generated with Perlin noise, training jerk and steering acceleration changes using PPO. During deployment, the BEV obtained from BEVFusion is circularly cropped, coordinate-aligned, and tracked by the real vehicle.
sections.details:
### II-A Simulator (MLR Simulator)
Rather than performing photorealistic 3D rendering, the simulator directly operates on semantic grid maps entirely on the GPU. There are only four classes: "Drivable" (paved/gravel roads), "Semi-drivable" (grass), "Non-drivable" (obstacles, stationary vehicles), and "None" (unknown areas). By layering multiple octaves of Perlin noise similar to Minecraft terrain generation, 3,800 diverse maps (500 m × 500 m, resolution 0.4 m) were automatically generated. Rough target paths (waypoints) are produced using graph search and moving-average smoothing (CCMA), and Gaussian noise is injected into the agent's initial position and steering angle to promote exploration and robustness.

### II-B Modeling and Reward Design
The input state to the policy network consists of an ego-centric BEV (60 m × 60 m, resolution 0.25 m, one-hot representation plus a waypoint rendering channel), vehicle state (velocity, acceleration, steering angle, steering velocity), previous action, target velocity, a sequence of 80 relative forward waypoints, and the remaining distance to the goal. These inputs are processed by CNN and MLP feature extractors, concatenated, and used to output actions.
The action space consists of two degrees of freedom in higher-order derivatives: jerk (rate of change of acceleration) and steering acceleration (rate of change of steering velocity). Each is discretized into 5 levels, forming a categorical distribution over 25 total actions. Because actions are integrated twice before affecting vehicle pose, smooth driving is achieved despite the discretization.
The reward function is based on progress along the path $\Delta s$, supplemented by terms matching target velocity, penalizing heading error, encouraging smoothness against sudden acceleration or sharp steering, maintaining distance from obstacles, and penalizing excessive speed when driving on grass.

### II-C Reinforcement Learning Setup
Built upon PPO, the system employs curriculum learning, starting with relaxed collision penalties that gradually increase in severity. Additionally, an undiscounted setting of $\gamma=1$ is intentionally used to discourage myopic behavior and promote globally safe driving without reckless shortcuts.

### II-D Deployment
On the real vehicle, BEVFusion estimates the real-world BEV from cameras and LiDAR. Because deviations arise between the real vehicle and the virtual vehicle in simulation, the ego-centric BEV is rotated and translated into the virtual vehicle's coordinate frame using homogeneous transformation matrices. A circular crop is applied during this step to prevent boundary artifacts caused by rotation. The virtual vehicle advances based on the policy's actions, and the real vehicle tracks the virtual vehicle's trajectory using longitudinal and lateral feedback controllers such as a Stanley controller. This full inference pipeline runs on an edge Jetson AGX Orin in an average of just 1.9 ms.

Green indicates drivable roads, yellow denotes semi-drivable areas like grass, and red represents obstacles, illustrating diverse automatically generated driving environments.

(A) The ego-centric BEV obtained from BEVFusion is (B) transformed into the virtual vehicle coordinate frame, and (C)(D) edge artifacts from rotation and translation are removed via circular cropping before entering the policy.

sections.heading: Real-world tests: clocking 33.6 km/h and fully autonomous driving across two vehicles
sections.summary: Evaluated on a demanding 3.0 km course using two real vehicles with differing wheelbases and weights, the system completed a total of 17.3 km without human intervention, achieving smooth high-speed driving up to 33.6 km/h and obstacle avoidance.
sections.details:
### III-A Simulation Training
Training was conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU for approximately 68 hours (over 1 billion samples and more than 2 million episodes). Dynamic and kinematic constraints were set conservatively below the physical limits of the real vehicle.

### III-B Real-World Evaluation Scenarios
Two test vehicles with different wheelbases and vehicle weights were used for experiments: MuCAR-4 (2.60 m / 1.8 t) and MuCAR-3 (2.86 m / 2.5 t). Training was performed exclusively using MuCAR-4 parameters, but the exact same trained model was deployed directly onto both vehicles. The 3.0 km track featured high-speed straightaways, shipping containers, trees, construction barriers, 180-degree hairpin turns, tall grass sections, and gravel roads.
Three consecutive laps were attempted with each vehicle, covering a total of 17.3 km. MuCAR-4 completed all three laps entirely without intervention, reaching a peak speed of 33.6 km/h on straight sections. It appropriately decelerated before sharp curves and around obstacles as guided by the reward design, exhibiting smooth behavior without severe hunting or oscillations. Furthermore, where waypoints were blocked by bollards, the vehicle autonomously found gaps between obstacles to bypass them. During MuCAR-3's third lap, rainy conditions and dusk lighting caused perception (BEVFusion) to overestimate obstacle sizes, resulting in a single safe stop when unable to pass through a narrow opening.

### III-C Ablation Studies
- **Perception gap evaluation**: Identical ideal BEVs generated directly from HD maps were compared against real BEVs from BEVFusion. When given ideal BEVs, the average speed difference between the two vehicles was only 0.150 m/s, confirming that the policy itself is highly robust to vehicle differences.
- **Impact of trajectory alignment**: When trajectory alignment was disabled and policy outputs were fed directly as control inputs to the real vehicle, time delays and friction caused severe oscillations; the vehicle failed to navigate the first curve and came to a stop in front of an obstacle.

captions.F6: Representative scenes from real-vehicle driving experiments. The vehicle smoothly navigates diverse conditions: reaching top speed of 33.6 km/h on straights (left), avoiding construction barriers and sharp turns (center), detouring through gaps to avoid bollards (top center), and autonomously decelerating on grass (top right).
captions.F8: Results of the control ablation experiment. When trajectory alignment was turned off and policy outputs were applied directly to the vehicle, latency and modeling errors caused delayed control in curves, leading to failure and stopping toward obstacles.

sections.heading: Remaining limitations: the gap to expert human driving and perception range limits
sections.summary: The policy did not acquire skilled maneuvers such as taking an 'out-in-out' racing line before hairpin curves, and the 60 m BEV perception range limits ultra-high-speed driving beyond 40 km/h due to the need for greater lookahead distances.
sections.details:
The experiments also highlighted several clear limitations.

First is the absence of expert-level driving maneuvers. The agent did not swing outward prior to entering 180-degree hairpin turns (the classic "out-in-out" line), nor did it maintain as much margin when evading a second barrier compared to the first. This stems from the exploration-safety tradeoff regarding how far the vehicle is permitted to deviate from the target path. Straying too far from the path carries the risk of encountering dead ends if obstacles appear later, causing the policy to remain conservative.

Second is the limit on achievable top speed. Even when the target speed was set above 40 km/h during training, the agent's peak speed plateaued. This is because the BEV sensing range is limited to 60 m centered on the vehicle (roughly 30 m forward). Under safety constraints of jerk at $-2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^3}$ and deceleration at $-2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, coming to a stop from 35 km/h requires a minimum braking distance of 28.4 m. Consequently, driving at higher speeds will require wider perception ranges and longer-range lookahead capabilities.

sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook: what lightweight mid-level representations bring to off-road RL
sections.summary: MILER achieved zero-shot Sim-to-Real transfer at over 30 km/h without heavy physics or 3D graphics simulators by combining semantic mid-level representations with trajectory alignment. Future work points toward leveraging human driving data and expanding into dynamic environments with other vehicles and pedestrians.
sections.details:
This paper presented MILER, an end-to-end framework for reinforcement learning autonomous driving in unstructured environments. By training policies in a lightweight semantic mid-level representation (MLR) simulator and extending trajectory alignment to spatial mid-level representations, zero-shot transfer to real vehicles was accomplished without any fine-tuning.

Extensive evaluations across two real vehicles proved that stable navigation of unfamiliar off-road courses is possible even above 30 km/h without vehicle oscillations. On the other hand, even with massive training on 1 billion samples, the policy did not automatically discover human-like racing techniques such as swinging wide before turns. The authors plan to explore incorporating human demonstration data and extending the framework to more complex environments featuring dynamic obstacles and other traffic participants.

takeaways: Off-road reinforcement learning does not require complex 3D graphics or detailed vehicle physics models; highly abstracted simulations using semantic BEVs and a 2-wheel bicycle model are sufficient.
Incorporating trajectory alignment—where the real vehicle tracks a simulated virtual vehicle—effectively neutralizes the Sim-to-Real gap caused by vehicle dynamics and latencies.
Setting the action space to higher-order derivatives (jerk and steering acceleration) ensures high real-world driving smoothness even with discrete action choices.
limitations: Strategic, dynamic driving maneuvers typical of human drivers—such as out-in-out lines through hairpin curves—are not self-learned by the agent.
The BEV perception range (~30 m forward) acts as a braking distance bottleneck, requiring longer-range lookahead before extending to speeds above 40 km/h.
Under adverse conditions like rain or dusk where BEVFusion segmentation accuracy degrades, misidentifying drivable space risks causing the vehicle to stall.
